INFERENCE SILICON · 1985 – 2026 · CYCLE RECONSTRUCTION × SECTOR DEEP DIVE

Forty-two years of
inference silicon

Is this time different?

From the Xilinx XC2064 in 1985 to the TPU v8 in 2026, the contest over who supplies custom compute has run for four decades. Three generations of challengers have entered; two clearing waves have swept through; the exit grammar has been acquisition-led — though not acquisition-only: the record carries one Chapter 11 restructuring en route to a sale. This report cuts forty-two years into six windows, reconstructs what was knowable at the time in each, and asks one question — is the 2023–2026 inference boom a replay of an old cycle, or a new cycle under a new set of constraints?

§1 · Executive summary

Is this time different?

Demand looks most like the 1995–2000 optical-networking boom, but the binding constraint has moved from wafer fabs to memory, packaging, and the power grid.

Every cycle in this report carries the same skeleton: demand becomes orders, orders become capacity, capacity becomes inventory, and the disappointment becomes clearing. What changes between cycles is where the system binds. In 2000 it bound at the fab — the FPGA duopoly rode optical networking up roughly three-fold, then gave back ≈−39% in a single reset. In 2025 it binds behind the fab: HBM stacks, CoWoS slabs, optical interconnect, and the grid interconnect queue.

The current expansion is the fastest revenue build in the industry's history: NVIDIA data-center revenue grew ≈17.6× from Q1 FY2024 ($4.28B, quarter ended April 30, 2023) to Q1 FY2027 ($75.2B) — twelve quarter intervals, thirteen quarterly observations. It is funded by the deepest capex program on record: the top four hyperscalers spent ≈$410–413B in 2025 (compiled estimate; company reports) and guide to $695–725B in 2026 — lifting capex/operating-cash-flow from 0.80 in 2025 to ≈1.21× for 2026E (range 1.18–1.24; guidance midpoints ≈$710B ÷ ≈$587B OCF, the OCF figure a working estimate — no public consensus aggregate exists).

The method is deliberately simple. Forty-two years are cut into six windows, each reconstructed as it was knowable at the time and graded against the present on five dimensions: demand composition, binding constraint, clearing mechanism, capital intensity, and software lock-in. Three gauges carry the argument — speed (17.6× against the optical boom's 3×), funding (capex against operating cash flow), and position (where the constraint sits). The instruction on every gauge is the same: watch the gates, not the headlines.

The verdict is refused as a single point. Two scenarios — a base case of ≈2.5× custom-silicon accelerator-revenue growth from 2025 to 2028E (a scenario, range ≈2.0–4.7×), against a contraction case of −15% to −35% — are handed to eight falsification triggers kept as a point-in-time register (research cutoff July 18, 2026): capex guidance, NVIDIA growth, HBM pricing, CoWoS utilization, custom-silicon dollar share, crossover units, the grid queue, and a disclosure row that remains a standing gap. The kill switch is explicit: Top-4 2027E capex growth below +14% voids the base case on contact, with no narrative rescue.

One discipline runs underneath: deploy first, disclose later. Production reality has run one to four years ahead of public knowledge since Catapult and the first TPU, so every 2026 announcement is read with that lag priced in — and the two standing gaps, the TPU unit range and the custom-versus-merchant dollar split, are carried open rather than estimated away.

§2 · Survivorship · 1975–2026

Three generations, one clearing grammar

Fourteen companies across three generations have contested custom compute. The selection variable was never the die. It was the software toolchain.

Read the graveyard before reading the boom — and read it against a stated cohort rule. The cohort tracked here is the AI-accelerator and FPGA startups founded 2010–2017 (the merchant wave), plus two named predecessors that contested the same market (Achronix, founded 2004; Wave Computing, founded 2008) and the two FPGA duopolists (Xilinx, Altera) kept for reference — fourteen companies, observed through July 18, 2026. The terminal outcomes resist the one-liner: six were acquired, one exited by asset sale, one completed a licensing transaction, one has gone public, and five still operate independently. Acquisition has been a common outcome in this selected cohort, but it has not been the only one; outcomes also include restructuring, dissolution, continued operation, licensing transactions, and public listing.

The texture is in the paths, not the totals. Wave Computing filed for Chapter 11 restructuring in 2020, emerged as MIPS in 2021, and was acquired by GlobalFoundries in 2025 — the cohort's only bankruptcy-law event, on the way to an exit. Nervana's product line was dissolved inside Intel in 2020, four years after its ≈$350M acquisition. Groq licensed its inference technology to NVIDIA in December 2025 — a reported ≈$20B (CNBC-reported, unconfirmed by NVIDIA) — with founders and engineers joining NVIDIA and the remnant still independent. Cerebras completed its IPO in May 2026 (Nasdaq: CBRS, priced at $185, ≈$5.5B raised). And Intel sold 51% of the Altera business to Silver Lake in September 2025, a decade after buying the company for $16.7B.

The generations sort cleanly. The FPGA duopolists cleared by acquisition across four decades — Altera to Intel for $16.7B in 2015, Xilinx to AMD for ≈$49B in 2022 — and both exits were rewards, not punishments. The named predecessors split: Achronix remains private and independent; Wave took the restructuring path to a sale. The merchant wave cleared fastest: Nervana to Intel, Habana to Intel ($2B, 2019), Graphcore to SoftBank (≈$600M reported, 2024), Flex Logix's technology assets and team to Analog Devices (2024) — while its surviving tail now spans five independents, one public company, and one licensing remnant. Consolidation is not a euphemism for failure in this record — it is how a losing toolchain gets folded into a winning portfolio.

Why does the toolchain select? Because custom silicon is bought as a compiler target, not as a chip. Actel, QuickLogic, Lattice, and Achronix all shipped credible silicon; the market sorted them on place-and-route quality, IP breadth, and migration cost — the same variable that later sorted Nervana, Habana, and Graphcore, and that is under test in the CUDA-versus-XPU contest today. An analyst in 2016 could see that CUDA was deep; the hard part was seeing that the depth, not the TOPS, was the asset being priced.

No liquidations — and no clean hands. No cohort member's terminal status is a dissolution or an unresolved restructuring — but “acquisition, never bankruptcy” would be false for this record: Wave Computing filed Chapter 11 in 2020 on its way to a sale, and Nervana's products were dissolved post-acquisition. The grammar bent; it did not break.

Note the direction of exit prices: the reference generation's flagship exits — $16.7B and $49B, seven years apart — bracket the shortage supercycle, and the merchant wave's disclosed clearings span ≈$350M to $2B, plus one reported ≈$20B license. When §9 prices a contraction scenario, this is the grammar it assumes: write-downs, acquisitions, and restructurings rather than liquidations.

§3 · Window one · 1985–1995 · The FPGA founding

“A better ASIC”: positioning as strategy

The FPGA did not win by being better silicon. It won by being a better purchasing decision — slower per gate, more expensive per gate, and nine months faster to market.

When Xilinx shipped the XC2064 in 1985, the part offered 64 configurable logic blocks — a rounding error against the gate arrays of the day, and a loser on every physical metric. What it sold instead was the elimination of the ASIC's fatal variable: the mask-spin, a foundry queue and a nine-month wait in which the market could move, compressed to a desk and an afternoon. Ross Freeman's framing — the FPGA as “a better ASIC” — was not a technical claim. It was a positioning decision, and positioning was the strategy: the FPGA's first market was the ASIC's regret.

The decade established the two facts that govern the rest of this report. First, the duopoly: Xilinx and Altera, founded a year apart, converged on the same architecture and split the market; challengers — Actel, QuickLogic, Lattice — survived only on ground the duopoly served badly. Second, the moat: as design sizes grew, the binding problem became place-and-route software, not transistors. Every design win added cells to the IP library, and every hour invested in one toolchain raised the cost of switching — the first appearance of the selection variable that decides every clearing in this report.

What was knowable by the window's close? That the FPGA had won prototyping and low-volume logic outright, that the toolchain was the asset, and that the parts were riding foundry curves into mid-volume sockets. What was not yet knowable was the demand shock that would stress the structure — the optical buildout still lay ahead.

From the record Paraphrase

Ross Freeman's pitch for the XC2064 was positioning, not physics: the part lost on every per-gate metric and won on the calendar — a custom-logic project compressed from a nine-month mask-spin to an afternoon at a desk. Xilinx's launch release of November 1, 1985 introduced the XC2064 as a “new class of ASIC” — the company framing its programmable part as the ASIC's substitute rather than its poor relation.

Ross Freeman · Xilinx co-founder, on the XC2064 positioning — summarized; the quoted fragment is from the Xilinx XC2064 press release, November 1, 1985

Context. Freeman's framing recast a physically inferior part as the economically superior choice — and became the industry's own description of itself.

Why it matters. Every challenger in this report faces Freeman's exam: not “is your chip better?” but “what does your chip let the buyer stop waiting for?”

Source ↗ · Company disclosure · Xilinx backgrounder (XC2064, Nov 1985)

§4 · Window two · 1995–2003 · Boom and bust

−39%: one shock, four different scars

Optical networking gave the duopoly its first real boom — roughly 3× revenue in five years — and its first real clearing. One shock, absorbed four different ways: Xilinx cut, Altera cut deeper, the customers vanished, and the suppliers ate the inventory.

The late-1990s optical buildout was, like the 2023 AI buildout, a real workload with a real revenue line and a capital structure that ran ahead of both. Xilinx revenue climbed from $560M in 1996 to $1,659M in fiscal 2001; Altera from $402M in 1995 to $1,377M in 2000 — with telecom customers concentrating both order books exactly where the bubble was most inflated. When carrier capex stopped in 2001, it did not slow — it stopped. Combined duopoly revenue fell ≈−39% in the reset, the fastest decline either company had ever recorded.

The anatomy is worth holding precisely: Xilinx cut headcount and defended the toolchain; Altera, skewed even harder toward communications, cut deeper; the customers did not trim but vanished as a demand source — which is why the reset printed as −39% rather than as a glide — and the supply chain absorbed the residue as inventory written down at every tier. Four instruments, one shock, none of them a bankruptcy court. (The revenue lines mix fiscal and calendar years, so the −39% is a derived, window-aligned figure.)

Two properties anchor the analogy to 2026. The demand was real — internet traffic roughly doubled annually; the error was extrapolating an S-curve into a straight line, and the double-ordering was invisible by construction, since each tier of the chain could see only its own backlog. And the exit grammar held: no major vendor liquidated, and the survivors emerged deliberately diversified. The question this report later puts to the AI cycle is not whether the demand is real — it plainly is — but whether the 2001 grammar still governs a market whose constraint has migrated from fabs to memory, packaging, and power.

From the record Paraphrase

Wim Roelandts's account of the 2001 reset, as Xilinx's chief executive, was that this was no ordinary slowdown: the orders did not decline — they stopped, and the inventory built for the ramp became the problem to manage. The filing record carries the shape of the boom he was describing: Xilinx revenue climbed from $662M in FY1999 to $1.02B in FY2000 and $1.66B in FY2001 — and then the reset arrived.

Wim Roelandts · Xilinx CEO, on the 2001 reset — summarized; revenue figures per Xilinx 10-K filings, FY1999–FY2001

Context. Xilinx's fiscal 2001 revenue of $1,659M fell sharply through calendar 2001 as carrier capex evaporated; Altera printed the same pattern a quarter earlier.

Why it matters. The 2001 reset is the template for this report's contraction scenario: a −15% to −35% path is what “the orders stop” looks like when the buyer is a capital market.

Source ↗ · Company disclosure · Xilinx 10-K filings (SEC EDGAR) · K17

§5 · Window three · 2004–2012 · The quiet decade

Deploy first, disclose later

Between the bust and the boom, the hyperscalers ran their first custom-compute experiments underwater. The pattern of the decade: production truth ran years ahead of public knowledge.

The canonical case is Microsoft Project Catapult: a research question became a 1,632-server pilot with an FPGA on every board, wired by the end of 2012 and disclosed at ISCA 2014 with a measured 95% throughput improvement on Bing ranking. The deployment predated the disclosure by well over a year. Rather than replacing CPUs, Microsoft placed reconfigurable fabric between server and network and partitioned the workload — what the fabric did well ran on the fabric; everything else stayed on x86. That template leads directly to Maia, just as the TPU's quiet work in this window's tail leads to Ironwood.

The disclosure lag has an economic logic, not merely a cultural one. A hyperscaler's custom silicon is a cost advantage over rivals renting the same merchant parts; publishing it invites replication and reprices the merchant's roadmap against you. Production truth therefore travels underwater until the advantage is spent or strategic to reveal — Google's 2016 disclosure arriving, not coincidentally, as its cloud business began courting outside customers.

The quiet decade is also this report's control group — the one window with no demand shock, which is why the analog matrix scores its demand row “none.” What accumulated underneath: CUDA's founding work in 2006–07, the TPU program's earliest gestation, Baidu's FPGA experiments. What was knowable in 2012: deep learning worked on GPUs, and one hyperscaler had proven reconfigurable acceleration at production scale. What was not: which of those two substrates the next decade would choose.

From the record Verbatim

“We describe a medium-scale deployment of this fabric on a bed of 1,632 servers.” Under high load, the fabric “improves the ranking throughput of each server by a factor of 95% for a fixed latency distribution — or, while maintaining equivalent throughput, reduces the tail latency by 29%.”

Andrew Putnam, Adrian Caulfield et al. · Microsoft Research, “A Reconfigurable Fabric for Accelerating Large-Scale Datacenter Services,” ISCA 2014

Context. The Catapult paper is the foundational disclosure of the cloud in-house era: FPGAs wired into a production tier, with a full accounting of throughput, cost, and failure behavior.

Why it matters. Catapult proved the hyperscaler in-house pattern a decade before the TPU made it famous — and established the deployment-disclosure lag this report treats as a law of the record.

Source ↗ · Company disclosure · historical record

§6 · Window four · 2013–2018 · Ignition

The TPU and the $16.7B check: two answers, one exam

Deep learning made inference a volume business. Two incumbents answered the same exam in opposite ways: Google built its own silicon and told no one for a year; Intel wrote the largest check in FPGA history.

The substrate event came first: AlexNet in 2012, two GTX-class GPUs winning ImageNet by a margin that ended hand-engineered vision — and the winning entry ran on CUDA. Within eighteen months the community's default substrate was merchant GPU silicon plus a proprietary software stack; every event in this window is a response to that decision. The Google answer was the TPU: deployed in production datacenters in 2015, disclosed in May 2016 as “a domain-specific architecture” for inference — by which time it had served search, translation, and photos for a year. The Intel answer was the Altera acquisition at $16.7B in June 2015: a bet that a third of cloud servers would carry an FPGA.

Underneath both answers sat the verdict that still governs the sector: the software ecosystem is the moat. CUDA, a decade deep by 2015, meant every challenger began life as an internal tool for a captive workload — the TPU line survived because Google was its own first customer at planetary scale. The eight generations below run from 92 TOPS in 2015 past Ironwood's 4,614 TFLOPS FP8 per chip and 9,216-chip pods (GA late 2025) to the TPU 8t/8i pair unveiled April 22, 2026 (GA later in 2026, estimate) — a log-scale climb that rivals the merchant line it was built to avoid buying.

Precision is the silent axis. 92 INT8 TOPS, 918 BF16 TFLOPS, and 4,614 FP8 TFLOPS are not three points on one line — each generation redefined the number itself.

The Intel answer failed slowly, then obviously. The thesis required hyperscalers to adopt a fabric whose toolchain they did not control; what they actually did was the Google move — hire silicon teams and design their own. The $16.7B check bought the duopoly's weaker half near the cycle's top; the stronger half would be repriced at $49B inside AMD seven years later. What remained unknowable in 2018: whether the in-house pattern would stay a Google eccentricity or become the industry default.

From the record Verbatim

“We've been running TPUs inside our data centers for more than a year, and have found them to deliver an order of magnitude better-optimized performance per watt for machine learning.”

Norm Jouppi · Distinguished Hardware Engineer, Google — “Google supercharges machine learning tasks with custom chip,” May 18, 2016

Context. The disclosure revealed that Google had deployed custom inference silicon in production since 2015, a full year before the industry learned of it.

Why it matters. The submarine pattern's canonical instance, and the founding document of the cloud in-house ASIC era that sections 9b–9f price out.

Source ↗ · Company disclosure · 2016 blog · ISCA 2017

From the record Verbatim

“Intel's growth strategy is to expand our core assets into profitable, complementary market segments. With this acquisition, we will harness the power of Moore's Law to make the next generation of solutions not just better, but able to do more.”

Brian Krzanich · Intel CEO, press release announcing the $16.7B Altera acquisition, June 1, 2015

Context. The largest check ever written for an FPGA franchise closed Intel's answer to the accelerator question — buy the fabric and the toolchain, and integrate both into Xeon.

Why it matters. The $16.7B tag is the market's first valuation of the inference-silicon supply line — the benchmark against which AMD–Xilinx at $49B repriced it.

§7 · Window five · 2019–2022 · Shortage and the M&A supercycle

The timing device

Shortage repriced everything. In 108 days the industry announced five billion-dollar deals; meanwhile the order grammar of scarcity — non-cancellable, non-returnable — quietly loaded the inventory correction that followed.

Between July and October 2020, five transactions each worth billions were announced in 108 days: ADI–Maxim, NVIDIA–Arm, SK hynix–Intel NAND, AMD–Xilinx, and Marvell–Inphi — well above $100B in headline value, the largest single-quarter consolidation on record. Scarcity is a timing device: it tells every CFO simultaneously that supply lines are strategic assets. AMD's $35B all-stock bid for Xilinx became a ≈$49B close in February 2022, repricing Intel's 2015 Altera check nearly threefold: the same asset class, one shortage later.

108 days. July 13 to October 29, 2020: ADI–Maxim, NVIDIA–Arm, SK hynix–Intel NAND, AMD–Xilinx, Marvell–Inphi. Scarcity compresses strategy into a quarter.

The demand side ran on NCNR orders — non-cancellable, non-returnable commitments placed 52 weeks out. NCNR is the order grammar of every shortage: rational for each buyer, destabilizing in aggregate, because it converts uncertain demand into certain backlog and then into certain inventory when demand pauses. Buyers ordered not what they needed but what they feared needing, and no instrument existed for measuring the overstatement — until consumer demand rolled over in 2022 and two years of visibility became two years of inventory to work down.

The correction followed the window's own grammar: nobody of consequence liquidated; the excess cleared through cancelled orders, written-down inventory, slashed wafer starts, and the M&A scarcity had already teed up. The lesson the window hands to 2026 is uncomfortable: the same structures now exist at ten times the dollars — prepaid HBM supply agreements, booked CoWoS slabs, take-or-pay power commitments — and they are exactly as unmeasurable from the outside as NCNR backlog was in 2021.

Interlude · 2017–2022 · The mining mirror

Crypto incubated custom silicon, then crashed it twice

Before the AI cycle, the mining cycle ran the same experiment twice at smaller scale: a workload so lucrative it pulled ASIC development forward by years — then reversed hard enough to saw the vendors' revenue lines in half.

Mining was the first workload to justify a full custom-silicon race at commercial scale: between 2013 and 2017 mining ASICs sprinted from 55nm to 16nm — four years of process technology absorbed in four years, because every joule saved per hash printed straight into margin — and reached 5nm by 2021. The lesson was double-edged: a sufficiently valuable workload can finance bleeding-edge custom silicon — and the same workload can vanish with a price chart, leaving a custom part with no second customer.

The two cycles cleared the same way. Cycle one: Bitcoin peaks near $19.7k in December 2017; panic ordering hits 16nm; the price collapse turns the order book into inventory, cleared through 2019. Cycle two: Bitcoin peaks near $69k in November 2021; GPUs themselves become the mining substrate — until the Ethereum merge of September 2022 ends GPU mining by protocol change, the only demand shock in this report delivered by software update. The shock propagated through three very different suppliers: NVIDIA misread the collapse and shipped a gaming quarter down 45% year over year — the famous crypto hangover; Alchip printed a literal sawtooth, annual revenue falling from NT$6.9B to NT$3.87B; GUC rode the same cycle with slower teeth across a broader book, from ≈NT$11.6B in 2017 toward ≈NT$24.9B by 2024.

The mirror's limits are as instructive as its reflections. Mining demand is speculative and software-free — a fixed-function hash with zero toolchain moat, which is why the analog matrix scores the mining row “none” on software lock-in. AI inference demand is contractual, multi-year, and compiler-bound: the amplitude lesson transfers, the duration lesson does not. Today's AI-ASIC vendors — two of them the same companies that printed the sawtooth — carry a different workload through the same plumbing; the mirror says the mechanism is intact and stays silent on the multiple.

From the record Verbatim

“The crypto hangover lasted longer than we expected. When prices went down, we expected demand to pick up more quickly.”

Jensen Huang · NVIDIA founder & CEO, Q3 FY2019 earnings call, November 15, 2018

Context. NVIDIA's Q3 FY2019 print missed its own guidance as crypto demand evaporated; the following quarter's gaming revenue fell 45% year over year. Demand that had looked like backlog turned out to be a price chart.

Why it matters. The mirror's demand-misreading lesson in the incumbent's own words — the same epistemic problem that NCNR backlog and today's prepaid capacity agreements repeat at larger scale.

Source ↗ · Company disclosure · earnings call, via Fortune (Nov 15, 2018) · K36

§8 · Window six · 2023–2026 · The current cycle

Demand, the shovel-sellers, and the migrating constraint

The fastest revenue build in industry history, funded by the deepest capex program on record. The question is no longer whether demand is real — it is what the demand is physically made of, and where that binds.

The capex anatomy rewards decomposition, because the aggregate hides a rotation. In 2021 the four hyperscalers spent $123.4B between them, mostly logistics infrastructure; by 2025 the total was ≈$410–413B (compiled estimate; company reports) — Amazon ≈$125B, Microsoft ≈$115B, Alphabet ≈$103B, Meta ≈$69.9B — and the increment is AI compute. One year's guided increment — roughly $280–310B — exceeds the entire 2024 spend. The supply chain is being asked to absorb a step-function, and step-functions are what gates are made of.

The funding side is the quieter story and the more important one, so state the basis precisely: the cohort is Amazon, Alphabet, Meta, and Microsoft, calendar-year with Microsoft calendarized; the 2026E capex figure is company guidance ($695–725B, midpoints ≈$710B), and the 2026E operating-cash-flow figure of ≈$587B is a working estimate — no public consensus aggregate exists. Top-4 OCF grew from $272.4B in 2021 to ≈$513B in 2025 — impressive, and insufficient against the guided build. The capex/OCF ratio ran 0.45–0.56 across 2021–2024, a band in which the build funds itself; printed 0.80 in 2025, on the caution line; and reaches ≈1.21× for 2026E — ≈$710B of guided capex against that ≈$587B OCF estimate, a range of 1.18–1.24 across the guidance band. On these estimates, aggregate capital expenditure would exceed aggregate operating cash flow, increasing dependence on balance-sheet liquidity, external financing, or reductions in other cash uses. What the ratio does not settle by itself is how the gap gets financed — cash buffers, debt issuance, leases, vendor financing, and working-capital swings each carry a share, and the mix matters more than the milestone. Those lines, not the ratio alone, say when the referee changes from customers to credit.

Free cash flow is the first stress gauge. Revenue can be bought with financed capex; free cash flow prints the financing. Watch it quarterly, company by company.

The constraint has migrated with each phase, and each migration moved the profit pool with it: GPUs gated 2023 (H100 supply was the surprise), CoWoS gated 2024 (capacity climbing ≈15kwpm to ≈38kwpm across the year), HBM and leading-edge wafers gated 2025 as packaging ramped into the ≈75–80kwpm class (third-party estimate), and the grid gates 2026 because it is the one gate capex cannot buy open on a two-year clock.

The incumbent is not standing still. NVIDIA's answer to the XPU wave is ecosystem breadth — and, in May 2025, an opening of the platform itself: NVLink Fusion, licensing its rack-scale fabric to third-party custom silicon. When the moat's owner starts selling bridges, the contest has moved from “GPU versus ASIC” to “whose fabric owns the rack.”

What is knowable today, by this report's own discipline? The revenue is real and audited quarterly; the capex is guided, and every revision so far has been a raise; the gates are observable through pricing and lead times. What is not knowable: the custom-versus-merchant dollar split inside each hyperscaler, the true unit volumes of the TPU program, and the durability of demand beyond the guided horizon. Window six is still inside its own submarine lag.

From the record Verbatim

“A tectonic shift is underway: for the first time in decades, data centers must be fundamentally rearchitected — AI is being fused into every computing platform. NVLink Fusion opens NVIDIA's AI platform and rich ecosystem for partners to build specialized AI infrastructures.”

Jensen Huang · NVIDIA founder & CEO, NVLink Fusion press release, Computex, May 19, 2025

Context. NVIDIA's answer to the XPU wave is to open the moat itself: NVLink Fusion lets third-party custom silicon — CPUs and XPUs from Fujitsu, Qualcomm, MediaTek, Marvell, Alchip and others — attach to NVIDIA's rack-scale fabric.

Why it matters. When the ecosystem's owner starts licensing bridges, the contest moves from “GPU versus ASIC” to “whose fabric owns the rack” — the platform question this report carries as K39–K41.

Source ↗ · Company disclosure · NVIDIA newsroom, May 19, 2025 · K39

§9 · Deep dives

The current cycle under the microscope

Five stress tests of the 2023–2026 cycle: the second in-house wave and how to count it, the 2027 crossover claim, the cadence mismatch, the four supply gates, and the constraint's last stop — the grid. Working hypothesis, untested on margin evidence: the profit pool sits at the gates, not in the cloud.

9B · Measurement discipline

The second in-house wave, and measurement discipline

A decade after the first TPU, every hyperscaler now fields its own silicon: Google's TPU v7 Ironwood ships 9,216 chips per pod at 42.5 FP8 exaFLOPS, AWS's Trainium 3 is the house's first 3nm AI chip, and Microsoft's Maia 200 and Meta's MTIA v3 extend the pattern — a second wave built for external-facing AI infrastructure, not just captive workloads.

When the in-house part becomes a product — Ironwood pods as rentable cloud inventory, Trainium positioned against merchant instances, Anthropic signed for up to 1M TPUs with >1GW of TPU capacity coming online in 2026 (October 2025 announcement) — the economics change from cost-avoidance to revenue, and the submarine lag compresses, because revenue wants marketing. But penetration can be counted three ways, and the three answers disagree by design.

By units, ASIC-class parts move from ≈30% of 2024 shipments toward a claimed ≈50% crossover in 2027F — the least informative basis, because a cloud ASIC at a fraction of a merchant GPU's price counts the same. By CoWoS allocation, the ASIC share runs ≈18% in 2024 toward ≈34% in 2027F — a forward indicator of capacity commitment. By dollar value — the only basis that touches revenue, margins, and capex stress — the custom-silicon share of accelerator-dollar spending (Series A, global accelerator-dollar scope, broker estimate) runs ≈8% in 2024, ≈12% in 2025, ≈16% in 2026F, ≈20% in 2027F. One claim, three answers — invasion, migration, or niche — depending on the ruler. Series A is also kept strictly separate from Series B, the third-party TSMC AI-revenue attribution of §9c: different numerator, different denominator, different institution — the two are never conflated, and only Series A enters scenario multiplication.

The dollar rule is not pedantry; it is what scenario arithmetic is made of. A demand multiple applies to a revenue base; margins and capex stress are denominated in money; the toll roads are paid per dollar of content, not per unit shipped. Unit counts still bound the fleet's physical capacity, and slabs booked today are shipped dollars two quarters out — but the three bases form a ladder from the physical to the financial, and analysis fails when the rungs are mixed.

9C · Deep dive

The 2027 crossover claim, stress-tested

The claim: custom ASIC units overtake GPU units in 2027. The arithmetic: broker unit models put the 2027 accelerator market at roughly 16–17 million GPU-equivalent parts, so a 50% unit share requires ≈8.0–8.4 million custom units in a single year — and because the TPU program is the only custom line with demonstrated capacity at that scale, the claim is, to a first approximation, a claim about Google's 2027 build-out. The requirement is not absurd — at 9,216 chips per pod, the 50% line is ≈870–910 pods of deployment in a year — but “not absurd” is not “established.”

Now look at the estimates for what the TPU program will actually ship: published figures span 6.5M to 15M units for 2026 — a range so wide the midpoint is meaningless. The low end fails the crossover test; the high end passes it in a single bound; both ends come from serious shops working the same supply-chain interviews — one camp counting wafer starts and packaging bookings, the other extrapolating from announced pod deployments.

The range is irreducible for three reasons. Allocation, not production: Google splits each TPU tranche between internal deployment and external cloud rental, a policy choice it can move quarter to quarter. Definitional drift: pod-bound chips versus rentable instances versus wafer starts. And the submarine pattern: the only party that knows the true number has never disclosed it. The verdict is therefore deliberately unsatisfying: unadjudicable on published evidence — meaning the crossover claim can be neither confirmed nor falsified from public data today. The missing evidence is specific: a disclosed unit figure, or an independent allocation audit. The trigger that would settle it is enumerable, below.

What would close the gap: a disclosed unit figure, teardown-anchored tallies converging within ±10%, or a CoWoS allocation audit that pins ASIC-camp wafer consumption independently. Until one arrives, the operative fact remains the dollar basis — a third-party TSMC AI-revenue attribution estimate (Series B, distinct from the Series-A accelerator-dollar share of §9b) of ≈66% GPU camp to ≈34% ASIC camp by 2027F; TSMC does not disclose an ASIC/GPU split, and its official disclosure is only that AI accelerators were a high-teens percentage of 2025 revenue — which says migration, not inversion, on the only ruler that enters scenario math.

9D · Deep dive

Why the cadence mismatch is manageable

Merchant GPUs ship on an annual cadence; cloud ASIC programs refresh roughly every two years. The mismatch is real, and it matters less than the cadence-gap argument claims — for four structural reasons. First, the operator core is stable: an in-house ASIC serves a bounded set of workloads whose shapes the operator controls, so the bar is not “best available” but “cheapest adequate” — a part that stays within striking distance on its own workloads keeps its fleet, which is why v5p remained economic deep into the Trillium ramp.

Second, engineering compression: chiplets, hardened SerDes, and reference boards have cut a new generation from a clean-sheet design to an integration exercise — Trillium arrived at 4.7× v5e peak compute on an annual cadence, and Ironwood followed roughly a year later. Third, compilers are the real cadence lever: most effective performance between hardware generations now arrives through the software stack, which ships weekly. Fourth, interconnect has decoupled scale from silicon cadence: pod-level fabrics let an operator add capacity by networking more of the previous generation — precisely what a 9,216-chip Ironwood pod demonstrates.

The honest counter-argument: annual merchant cadence does tax the in-house programs — in headcount, in stranded NRE when a generation slips, in the residual value of last year's fleet. “Manageable” is a claim about economics, not about ease, and it would be falsified by evidence that hyperscalers are throttling ASIC deployment because merchant parts have opened a durable, unbridgeable gap — evidence that would surface first in cloud instance pricing and in the crossover tallies of §9c. Nothing in the current record prints that.

9E · Deep dive · Four supply gates

Four supply gates — hypothesis: the profit pool sits at the gates, not in the cloud

Every dollar of AI demand must pass four physical gates: HBM, leading-edge process, CoWoS packaging, and optical interconnect — ordered here by rigidity, how slowly capacity responds to price. HBM is the most rigid: stacked DRAM with through-silicon vias, yields relearned each generation, 18-to-24-month qualification cycles, a supply base exactly three makers wide. The economics are already strange: HBM's share of DRAM revenue has run from ≈8% in 2023 toward ≈41% in 2027F on a fraction of the bits, and 2026 supply was largely booked a year ahead.

Capacity tells the same story: ≈113kwpm in 2022, ≈170 in 2023, ≈280 in 2024, ≈385 in 2025E, ≈460 planned for 2026E — a four-fold build that still trails the demand placed against it — while the stack climbs from 4-hi HBM1 to 12-hi HBM3E and 16-hi HBM4 in 2026E, pin speeds running ≈1.0 to ≈11Gbps. Each added layer is yield re-learned; that is why the gate relaxes slowly even at these prices.

CoWoS and the leading-edge process gate are a study in two kinds of scarcity. Packaging scarcity is arithmetic: capacity arrives in 10kwpm slabs — 12 in 2022, 15 in 2023, ≈38 in 2024, ≈75–80 by end-2025, with a 120–130kwpm target for end-2026 (third-party estimates; TSMC does not guide kwpm) — and bookings lead capacity by roughly two quarters, so the gate binds as hard as the slab staircase allows. Process scarcity is political economy: one foundry of record at 3nm-class, wafer agreements signed two to three years out, and a bypass — N−1/N−2 nodes with 2.5D compensation — costing a 20–30% performance-and-power tax.

Optical interconnect is the window-two gate returned for a second run: 800G is shipping, 1.6T is ramping, and the watch item is DSP supply — the same component family Marvell bought Inphi for in 2020. It is the least rigid gate today and the fastest-tightening, because pod-scale fabrics convert networking from plumbing into a performance multiplier: at 9,216 chips per pod, the fabric is the computer.

The investment-relevant consequence, stated as a hypothesis rather than a conclusion: hyperscaler capex is the tax base; the gates collect the tax. The durable franchises are those whose capacity cannot be replicated on the cycle's own clock — yield learning, the node lead, qualified lines, the optical DSP library. The hypothesis needs margin evidence it does not yet have: public filings do not segment gate-owner economics finely enough to prove where the pool settles, so the confirming or killing evidence is two years of segment-margin and ROIC disclosure across the chain. Until then the framing stands on capacity rigidity alone — which is why the six dossiers of §11 are populated by design houses and packaging-adjacent franchises, and why triggers 3 and 4 watch HBM pricing and CoWoS utilization rather than GPU benchmarks.

9F · Deep dive

The constraint's last stop: the grid

Follow the constraint far enough and it leaves the semiconductor industry entirely. The IEA's 2025 accounting puts datacenter electricity at 415TWh in 2024, rising to ≈945TWh by 2030 — more than double, with AI the largest single driver. The doubling is not exotic by historical standards; the concentration is: load arriving in single-campus, gigawatt-scale increments lands on grids planned for distributed, gradual growth. The 945TWh figure anchors the trigger framework — two stalled quarters of interconnect approvals at named sites would falsify it.

What makes the grid the terminal constraint is its cadence. HBM capacity quadruples in four years; CoWoS adds slabs quarterly; a leading-edge fab ramps in two to three years; a transmission interconnect study takes four to seven. Every upstream gate in this report can be bought open with enough capex; the interconnect queue cannot — it runs on regulatory time, measured in rights-of-way rather than purchase orders. This is why site selection has inverted: campuses now locate where power can be procured, and the compute follows the megawatts.

1GW ≈ 8,300 racks ≈ 600k packages ≈ 1.2M dies. The per-gigawatt ladder is the Rosetta stone between utility filings and semiconductor demand.

The rack-level arithmetic converts abstractions into queues. A GB200 NVL72 rack draws ≈120kW, so one gigawatt of AI capacity works out to ≈8,300 racks, ≈600,000 packages, ≈1.2 million dies, ≈$50B of all-in capex at a ≈$35k blended ASP, and ≈$2.1B of TSMC revenue. Multiply by the named commitments — Stargate at ≈7GW planned and $400B+ announced, against ≈0.6GW operational at Abilene on satellite-estimated reads; OpenAI–Oracle at 4.5GW, Meta's Hyperion at ≈5GW, xAI's Colossus, Amazon's Project Rainier — and the industry is discussing tens of gigawatts against queues that clear a handful per region per year. A demand-side disappointment would surface here first: in stalled campuses and renegotiated power agreements, filed in public.

Global electricity demand from data centres is set to more than double over the next five years, consuming as much electricity by 2030 as the whole of Japan does today.”

Fatih Birol · Executive Director, International Energy Agency — “Energy and AI” release, April 10, 2025

Why it matters. The official sector confirming that the binding constraint of the AI build has migrated off the wafer and onto the grid — the last gate, and the slowest one.

S10 · Deep dive · The consensus, stress-tested

Three bold assumptions

Every bullish 2027 deck rests on three load-bearing assumptions. Graded against the record: one fails, one is undecidable, and one arrives too late to verify.

A1 — where the AI dollar pools. The assumption holds that AI spending pools durably at the infrastructure layer, self-funded by operating cash flow. Scoped precisely, two claims hide inside it. The first — that custom silicon and merchant infrastructure are complements in the build, not substitutes — the record supports: every custom-silicon dollar arrives attached to merchant networking, memory, and power. The second — the pooling claim itself — fails only on the eligible dollar basis: custom silicon is ≈12% of 2025E accelerator dollars and ≈20% even in 2027F, so the pool stays ≈88% merchant on the basis that touches revenue. The self-funding clause fails on the funding record: capex/OCF reaches ≈1.21× for 2026E (range 1.18–1.24; OCF a working estimate), so on these estimates aggregate capital expenditure would exceed aggregate operating cash flow — increasing dependence on balance-sheet liquidity, external financing, or reductions in other cash uses. What would change the grade: custom share of accelerator dollars sustaining above ≈30% on the dollar basis (trigger 5), or two years of segment margin and ROIC disclosure showing the pool earns its cost of capital. Evidence grade: fail, as scoped — which does not end the cycle; it changes what would confirm it.

A2 — ASIC units overtake GPUs in 2027. The crossover claim of §9c: a 50% unit share needs ≈8.0–8.4M TPU-class units against published estimates of 6.5–15M. Evidence grade: undecidable. The concentration data cuts both ways — Broadcom's XPU franchise stands at six qualified customers plus two ramping, with ≈$73B+ of AI backlog, and Google its first and largest (exact share undisclosed): a real franchise, and a narrow one.

A3 — demand is visible to 2028. The assumption that multi-year backlog equals multi-year visibility. Evidence grade: late — the claim can only be tested by 2027–28 prints. Every program revision of the current cycle has been upward — Meta from $60–65B to $70–72B, Alphabet from $75B to $91–93B, Microsoft from ≈$80B to $140B+ annualized, Amazon from ≈$105B to ≈$125B — and a ledger that only revises up is evidence of momentum, not of visibility. The 2001 analogue is exact: carrier capex guides were raised through the peak quarter and into the first quarter of the reset. Hence “late,” not “false.”

The three grades are a method, not a mood. Fail means the record already contradicts the assumption on the basis that matters; undecidable means the published evidence cannot settle the claim in either direction; late means the deciding prints arrive after the window in which positioning decisions must be made. The practical use is triage: A1 makes trigger 5 the arbiter of the dollar migration; A2 leaves the crossover to trigger 6; A3 services every multi-year claim quarterly through triggers 1 and 2. The consensus is not the enemy of analysis here. Ungraded consensus is.

Hock Tan · Broadcom President & CEO, Q4 FY2024 earnings call, December 12, 2024

§9 · Verdict

Forty-two years in one table; the verdict in two scenarios

Seven historical windows scored against five dimensions — demand reality, constraint location, order grammar, clearing mechanism, and the software selection variable. Blue is same, hatch is partial, grey is none.

The matrix is the report's whole argument compressed to a grid. Read down the 2023–26 column: demand reality scores same as 1995–2000 — a physical workload growing at exponential pace, monetized ahead of its curve. Constraint location scores different — the binding gate has migrated from fabs to HBM, packaging, and power. Order grammar scores same — prepaid capacity and take-or-pay structures reproduce the 2019–22 epistemic problem at ten times the dollars. Clearing mechanism scores same — nothing suggests the acquisition-not-bankruptcy grammar has changed. And the software selection variable scores same — the toolchain still picks the survivors; what is contested in 2026 is whether CUDA's moat or the hyperscalers' captive scale is the deeper instance of it.

Four sames and one different: this cycle rhymes on almost every dimension that decided previous cycles, and differs precisely on the dimension that determines who collects the economics while it runs. No window matches on all five — the closest, 1995–2003, fails on software, because no CUDA-scale moat yet existed to select with; the mining mirror matches on clearing alone, because a fixed-function hash selects nothing.

The single “different” — constraint location — is the cell the whole report hangs on. Had the constraint stayed at the fab, this cycle would be a straight 1995–2000 replay: over-order, over-build, clear through consolidation. With the constraint at HBM, packaging, and power, three things change: a clearing arrives more slowly, because gates with two-to-seven-year response times do not mean-revert in a quarter; the beneficiaries differ, because gate owners hold the pricing power; and the early-warning instruments move from wafer bookings to memory pricing and interconnect queues. Same skeleton, different anatomy — which is why the verdict is two scenarios rather than one. Click any cell for the reasoning behind its grade.

Treat the 1995–2000 optical row as an analogy, not a template. Similar characteristics: a physical workload growing at exponential pace; capital spending that leads revenue; order books concentrated in a handful of buyers; a supplier base monetized ahead of the curve. Differing characteristics: the 2001 buyers were debt-financed carriers earning nothing from the asset, while 2026's buyers are the most profitable companies in history funding from operations — though the ≈1.21× 2026E capex/OCF ratio (OCF a working estimate) narrows that difference by the year; the demand is compiler-locked in a way optical transport never was; and the binding constraint sits behind the fab rather than at it. What would invalidate the analogy: evidence that inference revenue is failing to materialize at the application layer (trigger 2 breaking first), or a capex-guidance cut arriving while utilization is still rising — the 2001 signature ran in the reverse order. Until one prints, the analogy is the best available prior, held loosely.

§9 · Verdict · Scenario arithmetic

Scenario arithmetic: a ≈2.5× base case to 2028E — a scenario, not a forecast

Two scenarios, one kill switch — and one withdrawal. The base case is a scenario with stated assumptions, not a forecast: accelerator spending grows from $330B in 2025 (a derived working assumption, summed from vendor revenue lines) to $500B in 2028 (AMD's stated “>$500B by 2028” TAM claim — a company claim, not a consensus forecast), while the custom-silicon share of accelerator-dollar spending migrates from 12% (2025E, broker estimate) to 20% base — 16% low, 37% high on the JPM secondary path. The product is a custom-silicon accelerator-revenue multiple of ≈2.5× from 2025 to 2028E, range ≈2.0–4.7×. The conservative case holds the same spend path with the share stalled at the 2026F read (16%): ≈2.0×, band 1.9–2.1×. The contraction case is the 2001 grammar applied to 2026 dollars: a −15% to −35% path over three years, expressed through consolidation rather than bankruptcy, with the inventory correction landing first at the gates.

The kill switch is explicit: if Top-4 2027E capex growth falls below +14%, the base case is void — no narrative rescue, no re-anchoring. The threshold is not arbitrary: it is the growth rate below which the base case's spending path becomes arithmetically unreachable, so the scenario dies at the moment its own inputs fail rather than at the moment its holder loses conviction. That is what makes the framework a framework rather than a position.

The base-case chain is two multiplications on compatible denominators. Accelerator spending: $500B ÷ $330B ≈ 1.52×. Custom-silicon share of that spending: 20% ÷ 12% ≈ 1.67×. Product: ≈2.5×. The earlier version of this page multiplied total hyperscaler capex growth by a custom-silicon dollar share — inputs denominated in different dollars, since total capex also buys buildings, land, power, networking, storage, and general-purpose servers. That chain is withdrawn — incompatible denominators; the band it produced was not a valid result and should not be cited. What survives is the structure: two observable inputs and a kill switch.

2.5 ≈ 1.52 × 1.67. The base case is not a forecast of demand; it is the arithmetic consequence of two stated assumptions — and it dies with either of them.

The simplicity is the point. A model with twenty inputs can fit any narrative and falsify none; a model with two inputs and a kill switch can be wrong in public, cheaply. Every number in the chain is observable quarterly, and the eight triggers of §10 exist to move the probabilities before the prints do.

The dashed branch — the policy partition — is carried separately because neither scenario survives it intact. Export controls are splitting the accelerator market into two spheres with separate supply chains and separate clearing grammars; a partition amputates part of the addressable demand from both cases. It is drawn dashed because its probability is unpriceable from inside the record — pretending otherwise would be the one unfalsifiable move this report refuses to make.

§10 · Monitoring

Eight falsification triggers — a point-in-time register

A trigger reports what would kill the thesis — not what would flatter it. Each card carries its falsification condition, its current reading, and the next observation window. Click any card to open it.

Five triggers watch the money, three watch the gates, and one watches the crossover arithmetic directly. Each is written as a kill condition with a number attached: a capex-guidance cut below +20% year over year; two consecutive quarters of sub-+20% NVIDIA growth; HBM3E ASPs down more than 15%; CoWoS utilization below 85%; custom-silicon dollar share under 15% in the 2027F tallies; TPU unit estimates converging below 8.0M; a two-quarter stall in gigawatt interconnect approvals. Trigger 8 is the standing gap: the custom-versus-merchant dollar-split disclosure that no hyperscaler publishes.

Standing read: 1 confirmed (HBM sold-out) · 7 building/partial · 0 missing — point-in-time register, research cutoff July 18, 2026.

The statuses deserve a precise reading. “Partial” means the current reading is far from the kill line but the instrument is live; “1 confirmed” is the correct count for a young cycle, since confirmation is a property only mature supply squeezes possess — the HBM sold-out signal earned it. Read as a portfolio, the triggers cover the cycle's three failure modes in sequence: demand failure prints first in triggers 1 and 2, gate failure in 3, 4, and 7, and narrative failure — the crossover story dying in conversion to dollars — in 5, 6, and 8.

§11 · Company deep dives

Six companies on the supply chain's toll roads

If the profit pool sits at the gates, the investable question is who owns the toll roads. Six franchises, one table — expand any row for the full dossier.

The cohort spans the custom-silicon value chain. Broadcom (AVGO) is the design house of record — six qualified XPU customers plus two ramping, ≈$73B+ of AI backlog (Q2 FY26), and the networking franchise besides. Marvell (MRVL) is the second merchant design house, pairing its custom programs with the Inphi optical DSP annuity — the 2020 supercycle's most durable acquisition. MediaTek (2454.TW) brings handset-scale cost discipline to cloud ASIC programs. GUC (3443.TW) and Alchip (3661.TW) are the Taiwan design-service pair — the same two names that printed the mining sawtooth, now carrying cloud programs through TSMC's capacity plumbing. VeriSilicon (688521.SH) is the mainland entrant, relevant to any scenario in which supply chains regionalize.

The six names sort into three kinds of toll road. The merchant design houses sell the whole bridge — co-design methodology, SerDes IP, turnkey production, priced as NRE plus per-unit silicon; Broadcom's franchise is the deeper and the narrower, with Google its first and largest XPU customer (share undisclosed). The TSMC-aligned pair sell the door to the gate: design service plus adjacency to leading-edge capacity, with NRE that leads revenue by one to two years. MediaTek is the second-source challenger; VeriSilicon is the partition play, whose moat and whose risk are the same fact.

Two disciplines apply throughout. Customer concentration is treated as risk, not validation: a franchise whose AI revenue rides on one buyer is a toll road with a single vehicle, and engaged-prospect pipelines are options, not revenue. And every dossier's risk cell is an observable wired back to §10 — Broadcom's Google concentration watches trigger 5's dollar share; Marvell's timing, MediaTek's pricing, GUC's NRE cyclicality, Alchip's concentration, VeriSilicon's partition exposure each map to the trigger that would kill the thesis first.

Method, gaps, and sources

Every figure in this report traces to a dated source or is marked as derived, estimate, or gap. The register below is the audit trail; the method notes explain the counting rules.

Measurement discipline

Penetration is counted three ways — units, CoWoS allocation, and dollar value — and the three bases are never mixed; only the dollar basis enters scenario multiplication. Precision bases (INT8, BF16, FP8, FP4) are flagged wherever compute figures are compared, and log scales wherever generations span orders of magnitude. Where a number is computed from others it is marked derived; where it rests on broker or supply-chain estimation, estimate; where no auditable figure exists, gap.

Gaps

Two gaps are load-bearing and are carried as standing rows rather than papered over. K34: no external arbiter — a disclosed unit figure, a teardown-anchored tally, or a CoWoS allocation audit — yet exists to settle the crossover claim, which is why §9 stays unadjudicable (K35) and the eighth trigger stays unmeasurable by construction. K40: no confirmed NVIDIA-designed custom die exists in the public record; the platform question is carried as a watched absence, not a rumor.

Source classes

AI-assisted research Aggregations, derivations, and adjudications produced for this report from primary material.

Broker research Sell-side models: unit tallies, capacity trackers, attribution reads. Treated as estimate.

Company disclosure Filings, calls, papers, and product documentation. The primary record.

Industry & official IEA and official statistics; trade-press reporting where no filing exists.

Disclaimer

This report is for information only and is not investment advice, an offer, or a solicitation. Figures marked estimate, forecast, or derived may prove wrong; figures marked gap are known to be missing. Historical patterns — including the acquisition-not-bankruptcy clearing grammar — are descriptions of a record, not guarantees of repetition. The scenario arithmetic is a framework for thinking, not a price target.

State taxonomy

Every register row carries one of five states, enforced as rules. Actual: printed in a filing or official release. Estimate: a serious outsider's number where no filing exists. Forecast: a stated guidance range or plan, treated as a claim about the future. Derived: arithmetic on other rows, reproducible from them — the −39% reset, the 17.6× run, the per-gigawatt ladder. Gap: a number that does not exist in auditable form, carried as a row, never interpolated into silence.

Counting caveats

Three caveats recur. Fiscal years: Xilinx reports on a spring fiscal year, Altera on the calendar; window-aligned figures are marked derived for that reason. Ranges versus points: where the record supports only a range — TPU units, capex guidance, scenario multiples — the report publishes the range and refuses the false precision of a midpoint. Quotations: every quotation on this page is verbatim from the cited source; summaries without quotation marks are paraphrase and are tagged as such.

How to read the register

The register below is the audit trail, not a bibliography. Its forty-one rows are the load-bearing facts — the ones the scenarios, grades, and triggers actually consume — selected by a single test: would removing this number change a verdict? K1–K5 carry the scenario framework and the capex aggregate; K6–K9 the penetration bases; K10 the merchant benchmark; K11–K16 CoWoS and the HBM gate; K17–K18 the 2001 record; K19–K22 TPU units and per-gigawatt economics; K23–K26 the custom vendors and the grid; K27–K35 the merchant-adjacent record, capex stress, and the crossover test; K36–K38 the mining mirror; K39–K41 the platform-opening questions. Every ◆ anchor in the body resolves to one of these rows.
